claim: Serial dependence describes the phenomenon that current object representations are attracted to previously encoded and reported representations.
source: Serial dependence describes the phenomenon that current object representations are attracted to previously encoded and reported representations.
evidence: This is a definitional statement from the abstract that establishes what serial dependence is based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Attractive biases have been observed reliably in behavior.
source: While attractive biases have been observed reliably in behavior, a direct neural correlate has not been established.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the field without specific citations in this sentence, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: A direct neural correlate of serial dependence has not been established.
source: While attractive biases have been observed reliably in behavior, a direct neural correlate has not been established.
evidence: This statement summarizes the state of the field based on inference from prior literature.

claim: Previous studies have shown a reactivation of past information without observing a neural signal related to the bias of the current information.
source: Previous studies have either shown a reactivation of past information without observing a neural signal related to the bias of the current information, or a repulsive distortion of current neural representations contrasting the behavioral bias.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from previous research, implicitly referencing prior studies.

claim: Previous studies have shown a repulsive distortion of current neural representations contrasting the behavioral bias.
source: Previous studies have either shown a reactivation of past information without observing a neural signal related to the bias of the current information, or a repulsive distortion of current neural representations contrasting the behavioral bias.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from previous research, implicitly referencing prior studies.

claim: The present study recorded neural signals with magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a working memory task.
source: The present study recorded neural signals with magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a working memory task to identify neural correlates of serial dependence.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: Participants encoded and memorized two sequentially presented motion directions per trial.
source: Participants encoded and memorized two sequentially presented motion directions per trial, one of which was later retro-cued for report.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: Multivariate analyses provided reliable reconstructions of both motion directions.
source: Multivariate analyses provided reliable reconstructions of both motion directions.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis in the current study.

claim: The reconstructed directions in the current trial were attractively shifted toward the target direction of the previous trial.
source: Importantly, the reconstructed directions in the current trial were attractively shifted toward the target direction of the previous trial.
evidence: This is a key finding from the data analysis in the current study.

claim: The neural bias mirrored the behavioral attractive bias, thus reflecting a direct neural signature of serial dependence.
source: This neural bias mirrored the behavioral attractive bias, thus reflecting a direct neural signature of serial dependence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the observed data.

claim: The neural bias emerged at later, post-encoding time points.
source: The use of a retro-cue task in combination with MEG allowed us to determine that this neural bias emerged at later, post-encoding time points.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of the MEG data.

claim: Serial dependence in working memory affects memorized information during read-out and reactivation processes that happen after the initial encoding.
source: This timing suggests that serial dependence in working memory affects memorized information during read-out and reactivation processes that happen after the initial encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing data from the study.

claim: Serial dependence is the phenomenon that a current visual object is reported as more similar to a previously encountered visual object than it actually was.
source: This coherence is thought to be supported by serial dependence (Fischer and Whitney, 2014), that is, the phenomenon that a current visual object is reported as more similar to a previously encountered visual object than it actually was.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation to Fischer and Whitney, 2014.

claim: The attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are close in time and space.
source: This attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are close in time and space, that are attended, and that are similar to each other both with regard to the visual feature that has to be recalled and with regard to accompanying context features (Czoschke et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020; Fischer and Whitney, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are attended.
source: This attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are close in time and space, that are attended, and that are similar to each other both with regard to the visual feature that has to be recalled and with regard to accompanying context features (Czoschke et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020; Fischer and Whitney, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are similar to each other with regard to the visual feature that has to be recalled.
source: This attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are close in time and space, that are attended, and that are similar to each other both with regard to the visual feature that has to be recalled and with regard to accompanying context features (Czoschke et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020; Fischer and Whitney, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are similar to each other with regard to accompanying context features.
source: This attractive bias acts most strongly between current and previous objects that are close in time and space, that are attended, and that are similar to each other both with regard to the visual feature that has to be recalled and with regard to accompanying context features (Czoschke et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020; Fischer and Whitney, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including encoding.
source: Furthermore, serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including encoding (Murai and Whitney, 2021), memorization (Bliss et al., 2017), and read-out or decision (Fritsche et al., 2017; Pascucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Murai and Whitney, 2021.

claim: Serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including memorization.
source: Furthermore, serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including encoding (Murai and Whitney, 2021), memorization (Bliss et al., 2017), and read-out or decision (Fritsche et al., 2017; Pascucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bliss et al., 2017.

claim: Serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including read-out or decision.
source: Furthermore, serial dependence occurs at different levels of object processing including encoding (Murai and Whitney, 2021), memorization (Bliss et al., 2017), and read-out or decision (Fritsche et al., 2017; Pascucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fritsche et al., 2017 and Pascucci et al., 2019.

claim: Single-unit recordings from monkey prefrontal cortex combined with electroencephalography (EEG) and transcranial magnetic stimulation in humans have demonstrated that information about a previous stimulus was reactivated shortly before a new stimulus was encoded.
source: Single-unit recordings from monkey prefrontal cortex combined with electroencephalography (EEG) and transcranial magnetic stimulation in humans have demonstrated that information about a previous stimulus was reactivated shortly before a new stimulus was encoded (Barbosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Barbosa et al., 2020.

claim: The strength of pre-encoding reactivation in the prefrontal cortex predicted the attractive bias of the behavioral response to the new stimulus.
source: This study found that the strength of this pre-encoding reactivation in the prefrontal cortex predicted the attractive bias of the behavioral response to the new stimulus.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Barbosa et al., 2020 study.

claim: Subjects showed an enhanced serial bias after single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation of their prefrontal cortex.
source: Moreover, subjects showed an enhanced serial bias after single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation of their prefrontal cortex, which further supported a causal link between the observed reactivation and serial dependence.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Barbosa et al., 2020 study.

claim: Memory traces from previous trials recorded from the posterior parietal cortex in rats reappeared during the inter-trial interval (ITI) of a working memory task.
source: Another study (Akrami et al., 2018) showed that memory traces from previous trials recorded from the posterior parietal cortex in rats reappeared during the inter-trial interval (ITI) of a working memory task, were present throughout the next trial, and predicted the behavioral bias.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Akrami et al., 2018.

claim: Memory traces from previous trials were present throughout the next trial.
source: Another study (Akrami et al., 2018) showed that memory traces from previous trials recorded from the posterior parietal cortex in rats reappeared during the inter-trial interval (ITI) of a working memory task, were present throughout the next trial, and predicted the behavioral bias.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Akrami et al., 2018.

claim: Memory traces from previous trials predicted the behavioral bias.
source: Another study (Akrami et al., 2018) showed that memory traces from previous trials recorded from the posterior parietal cortex in rats reappeared during the inter-trial interval (ITI) of a working memory task, were present throughout the next trial, and predicted the behavioral bias.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Akrami et al., 2018.

claim: Frontal and parietal regions are involved in the storage of memory traces and their transfer into current processing.
source: The observed results indicate that frontal and parietal regions are involved in the storage of memory traces and their transfer into current processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on reactivation.

claim: Several human EEG studies have shown reactivation signatures of the previous stimulus or a response during the current trial.
source: Several human EEG studies have also shown reactivation signatures of the previous stimulus or a response during the current trial, establishing reactivation as an important neural prerequisite for the emergence of serial dependence (Bae and Luck, 2019; Barbosa et al., 2020; Fornaciai and Park, 2018; Fornaciai and Park, 2020; Fornaciai et al., 2023; Luo and Collins, 2023; Ranieri et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to EEG studies.

claim: Reactivation is an important neural prerequisite for the emergence of serial dependence.
source: Several human EEG studies have also shown reactivation signatures of the previous stimulus or a response during the current trial, establishing reactivation as an important neural prerequisite for the emergence of serial dependence (Bae and Luck, 2019; Barbosa et al., 2020; Fornaciai and Park, 2018; Fornaciai and Park, 2020; Fornaciai et al., 2023; Luo and Collins, 2023; Ranieri et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple cited EEG studies.

claim: Neural activity in the visual cortex measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was influenced by orientations presented on a previous trial during the encoding and maintenance of a current orientation.
source: Neural activity in the visual cortex measured with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was influenced by orientations presented on a previous trial during the encoding and maintenance of a current orientation (St. John-Saaltink et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to St. John-Saaltink et al., 2016.

claim: The current neural representation of an orientation in the visual cortex was repulsed from an orientation remembered in the previous trial.
source: In a more recent fMRI study (Sheehan and Serences, 2022), the current neural representation of an orientation in the visual cortex was repulsed from an orientation remembered in the previous trial, which was in contrast to an observed behavioral attraction.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sheehan and Serences, 2022.

claim: A recent magnetoencephalography (MEG) study observed a neural repulsion of a current representation during encoding, in contrast to a behavioral attractive bias toward past information.
source: In line with this finding, a recent magnetoencephalography (MEG) study (Hajonides et al., 2023) observed a neural repulsion of a current representation during encoding, in contrast to a behavioral attractive bias toward past information.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hajonides et al., 2023.

claim: The attractive behavioral bias is driven by post-encoding processes.
source: The authors of both studies proposed that the attractive behavioral bias is driven by post-encoding processes.
evidence: This is a proposal from cited studies (Sheehan and Serences, 2022; Hajonides et al., 2023).

claim: Early visual representations are repulsed and the behavioral attraction emerges during post-encoding read-out of memorized information.
source: This view is supported by another computational model (Fritsche et al., 2020), which states that early visual representations are repulsed and the behavioral attraction emerges during post-encoding read-out of memorized information.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a computational model by Fritsche et al., 2020.

claim: A direct reflection of the attractive bias of current information on the neural level has not been observed.
source: Until now, a direct reflection of the attractive bias of current information on the neural level has not been observed, and it has remained unclear during which processing step memory representations are actually biased toward the past.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the field based on the reviewed literature.

claim: It has remained unclear during which processing step memory representations are actually biased toward the past.
source: Until now, a direct reflection of the attractive bias of current information on the neural level has not been observed, and it has remained unclear during which processing step memory representations are actually biased toward the past.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of the field based on the reviewed literature.

claim: Ten human participants (seven females) memorized two sequentially presented visual objects per trial while their neural signals were measured via MEG.
source: Ten human participants (seven females) memorized two sequentially presented visual objects per trial (S1 and S2), while their neural signals were measured via MEG.
evidence: This describes the participants and methodology of the current study.

claim: Each participant completed two sessions with a total of 1022 trials.
source: Each participant completed two sessions with a total of 1022 trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: Serial dependence toward the target of the previous trial was observed, as the reported target motion direction of the current trial was systematically attracted to the retro-cued motion direction of the previous trial.
source: As expected, we observed a serial dependence toward the target of the previous trial, as the reported target motion direction of the current trial was systematically attracted to the retro-cued motion direction of the previous trial.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the current study's data.

claim: The attraction followed a derivative-of-Gaussian (DoG)-shaped curve with an amplitude parameter of 3.51°.
source: This attraction (Figure 1b) followed a derivative-of-Gaussian (DoG)-shaped curve with an amplitude parameter of 3.51° (bootstrapped SD: 0.479°, lower 95% of permutations between –3.51° and 2.03°, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.236) and a w parameter of 0.024, equaling a width of 47.37° (full width at half maximum, FWHM).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data analysis, also shown in Figure 1b.

claim: No significant serial dependence toward the non-target of the previous trial was observed.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a significant serial dependence toward the non-target of the previous trial (amplitude: –1.02°, bootstrapped SD: 0.788°, middle 95% of permutations between –1.63 and 1.49, p = 0.206, R2 = 0.014; w parameter: 0.046, equaling 24.53° FWHM), which replicated our previous observations (Czoschke et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis that replicates prior work.

claim: Serial dependence was modulated by task-relevant color.
source: Serial dependence was modulated by task-relevant color.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Serial dependence was stronger when the current item had the same color as the cued item of the previous trial than when their colors differed.
source: It was stronger when the current item had the same color as the cued item of the previous trial (amplitude = 4.02°, SD = 0. 528°, lower 95% of permutations between –3.70° and 2.41°, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.167) than when their colors differed (amplitude = for all three epochs, we observed 2.99°, SD = 0. 538°, lower 95% of permutations between –2.99° and 1.79°, p = 0.001, R2 = 0.106).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The amplitude difference between same-color and different-color conditions amounted to 1.02°, p = 0.038.
source: The amplitude difference amounted to 1.02°, p = 0.038.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The context effect found in the current study replicated a previous study.
source: This replicated the context effect found in our previous study (Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement connects the current finding to a prior publication.

claim: An inverted encoding model (IEM) was applied to the MEG data from all active sensors (271) within defined time windows of 100 ms length.
source: We applied an IEM (Brouwer and Heeger, 2009; Brouwer and Heeger, 2011; Sprague and Serences, 2013) to the MEG data from all active sensors (271) within defined time windows of 100 ms length.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used in the current study, with citations to the IEM technique.

claim: An encoding model with 18 motion direction-selective channels was constructed.
source: Specifically, we constructed an encoding model with 18 motion direction-selective channels.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the analysis method.

claim: Successful reconstructions of the corresponding motion directions were observed for all three epochs (S1 epoch, S2 epoch, and retro-cue epoch).
source: For all three epochs, we observed successful reconstructions of the corresponding motion directions with a fidelity significantly greater than zero (S1 epoch: p < 0.002, cluster extent: 300–1200 ms, mean fidelity = 0.139; S2 epoch: p < 0.002, cluster extent: 0–1300 ms, mean fidelity = 0.120; retro-cue epoch: p < 0.002, cluster extent: 300–1500 ms, mean fidelity = 0.115) (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: The information about the motion direction of S1, S2, and the retro-cued target was represented in the neural signals during the respective epochs.
source: This shows that the information about the motion direction of S1, S2, and the retro-cued target was represented in the neural signals during the respective epochs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the successful reconstruction results.

claim: During the S2 epoch, the direction of S1 could be successfully reconstructed with a fidelity significantly greater than zero.
source: We observed that during the S2 epoch, the direction of S1 could be successfully reconstructed with a fidelity significantly greater than zero (S1 during S2 epoch: p = 0.005, pBonferroni = 0.015, cluster extent: 100–700 ms, mean fidelity = 0.065).
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The mean fidelity of S1 during S2 epoch was significantly smaller than the fidelities of the currently relevant direction during all other epochs.
source: However, its mean fidelity within the significant cluster was significantly smaller than the fidelities of the currently relevant direction during all other epochs, that is, S1 during S1 epoch, S2 during S2 epoch, and target during the retro-cue epoch (all p-values below 0.005).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The information about the non-target item could not be reconstructed in the retro-cue phase.
source: As expected, the information about the non-target item could not be reconstructed in the retro-cue phase (all cluster p-values >0.05).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The shift of the mean reconstruction of the first item did not differ from 0° for the S1 epoch.
source: We found that the shift of the mean reconstruction of the first and second item did not differ from 0° for the S1 epoch (–2.83°, p = 0.743, bootstrapping test, pFDR = 0.870, 95% of permutations between –11.60° and 6.00°)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the MEG data analysis regarding neural shifts.

claim: The shift of the mean reconstruction of the second item did not differ from 0° for the S2 epoch.
source: or for the S2 epoch (–2.50°, p = 0.870, bootstrapping test, pFDR = 0.870, 95% of permutations between –7.57° and 2.11°), respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the MEG data analysis regarding neural shifts.

claim: For the retro-cue epoch, the mean reconstruction of the current target was shifted toward the previous target.
source: In contrast, for the retro-cue epoch, we found that the mean reconstruction of the current target was shifted toward the previous target (10.22°, p = 0.009, bootstrapping test, pFDR = 0.026, 95% of permutations between 1.64° and 21.97°; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a key finding from the MEG data analysis, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There was an attractive shift of the S1 direction toward the target of the previous trial during the S2 epoch.
source: In addition, there was an attractive shift of the S1 direction toward the target of the previous trial during the S2 epoch (11.69°, p < 0.001, bootstrapping test, 95% of permutations between 4.96° and 31.06°; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis, also shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The MEG data provided evidence for an attractive distortion of current neural representations toward the target information in the previous trial.
source: Thus, our MEG data provided evidence for an attractive distortion of current neural representations toward the target information in the previous trial, thereby revealing a direct neural signature of serial dependence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: The reconstructed shift of the retro-cued target item during the retro-cue phase predicted the upcoming behavior between 400 and 800 ms after the onset of the retro-cue.
source: Indeed, Figure 4 shows that the reconstructed shift of the retro-cued target item during the retro-cue phase predicted the upcoming behavior between 400 and 800 ms after the onset of the retro-cue (p = 0.003, permutation test, pBonferroni = 0.009; mean r = 0.030).
evidence: This is a correlation finding from the MEG and behavioral data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: There were no significant correlations for any other time points during the S1 and S2 epochs.
source: In contrast, there were no significant correlations for any other time points during the S1 and S2 epochs (cluster-based permutation test exact test, one-tailed).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: There were no significant correlations of the S1 reconstruction with the response error during the S2 epoch.
source: While the maximum of the S1 reconstruction also showed a significant shift toward the previous target, there were no significant correlations of the S1 reconstruction with the response error during the S2 epoch (no clusters with a p-value <0.05).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The information about the previous target was reactivated just prior to the onset of the next trial.
source: Consistent with previous findings from monkey single cell and human EEG recordings (Barbosa et al., 2020), we observed that the information about the previous target was reactivated just prior to the onset of the next trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis that replicates prior work.

claim: Direction reconstructions showed a fidelity significantly greater than zero during a time period at the end of the ITI.
source: Direction reconstructions showed a fidelity significantly greater than zero during a time period at the end of the ITI (p = 0.019, cluster extent: –200 to 100 ms (relative to S1 onset), mean fidelity = 0.069).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The target from the previous trial was reactivated once more at a later time period during the current trial, when the retro-cue indicated which item of the current trial was the target for the upcoming response.
source: Interestingly, we found that the target from the previous trial was reactivated once more, but at a later time period during the current trial, that is, when the retro-cue indicated which item of the current trial was the target for the upcoming response (p = 0.040, cluster extent: 2700–2900 ms relative to trial onset, mean fidelity = 0.057).
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: No evidence of previous target reactivations was found during the encoding or maintenance of current items.
source: In contrast, we found no evidence of previous target reactivations during the encoding or maintenance of current items (no clusters with a p-value <0.05).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Gaze directions were systematically related to presentation and memorization of the stimulus direction (S1 and S2 epoch) and its cue-based retrieval (retro-cue phase).
source: We found that gaze directions were systematically related to presentation and memorization of the stimulus direction (S1 and S2 epoch) and its cue-based retrieval (retro-cue phase).
evidence: This is a finding from the eye-tracking control analysis.

claim: Gaze directions varied considerably between subjects.
source: They also varied considerably between subjects.
evidence: This is a finding from the eye-tracking control analysis.

claim: Gaze directions were not systematically related to the MEG data.
source: Most importantly, gaze directions were not systematically related to the MEG data, thus ruling out that they had mainly driven our MEG results.
evidence: This is a finding from the eye-tracking control analysis.

claim: The current study provides the first evidence for an attractive bias of neural representations in the current trial toward information from the previous trial.
source: More importantly, our study provides the first evidence for an attractive bias of neural representations in the current trial toward information from the previous trial, which mirrors the behavioral effects of serial dependence and as such represents a neural signature of serial dependence.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's contribution based on the data.

claim: The reactivation of past information in the current trial is crucial because an attractive bias can only occur when information from the past has left a memory trace that interacts with the processing of the current object.
source: The reactivation of past information in the current trial is crucial because an attractive bias can only occur when information from the past has left a memory trace that interacts with the processing of the current object.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the necessity of reactivation for serial dependence.

claim: The memory trace of the previous target was reactivated just prior to the onset of the current trial and later in the current trial after the retro-cue indicated the current target.
source: Similar to the previous studies, we also found that the memory trace of the previous target was reactivated just prior to the onset of the current trial and later in the current trial after the retro-cue indicated the current target.
evidence: This is a summary of the reactivation findings from the current study.

claim: The combination of a retro-cue paradigm with the high temporal resolution of MEG accounts for the successful demonstration of serial dependence at the neural level in the present study.
source: We propose that our combination of a retro-cue paradigm with the high temporal resolution of MEG accounts for the successful demonstration of serial dependence at the neural level in the present study.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why the current study succeeded where others did not.

claim: Sheehan and Serences, 2022 proposed a computational model in which early encoding-related signals are repulsed from the recent past.
source: The authors proposed a computational model in which early encoding-related signals are repulsed from the recent past.
evidence: This describes a model from a cited study.

claim: According to Sheehan and Serences, 2022, the attraction observed in behavior was attributed to a later decoding process that overcomes the repulsion of sensory signals.
source: The attraction observed in behavior was attributed to a later decoding process that overcomes the repulsion of sensory signals and leads to serial dependence but is not directly detectable in hemodynamic response patterns.
evidence: This describes a proposal from a cited study.

claim: According to an ideal observer model, a repulsive bias occurs early during encoding, whereas an attractive bias is due to the read-out of the current object representation in a Bayesian history-dependent manner.
source: According to this model, a repulsive bias occurs early during encoding, whereas an attractive bias is due to the read-out of the current object representation in a Bayesian history-dependent manner.
evidence: This describes a model from Fritsche et al., 2020.

claim: Fritsche et al., 2017 found a repulsive bias in a perception task when the grating was still visually present, whereas in a working memory task, the current target orientation was attracted toward the orientation reported in the preceding trial.
source: Fritsche et al., 2017, for example, asked participants either to remember and report the orientation of a grating after a short delay (working memory task) or to compare two simultaneously presented orientations directly (perception task). They found a repulsive bias in the perception task, when the grating was still visually present and compared to another grating, whereas in the working memory task, the current target orientation was attracted toward the orientation reported in the preceding trial.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited behavioral study.

claim: The present study provided support for the notion that the neural markers of serial dependence occur during post-perceptual phases of a working memory task.
source: The present study provided support for the notion that the neural markers of serial dependence occur during post-perceptual phases of a working memory task, which is in agreement with existing models and behavioral findings (Fritsche et al., 2020; Hajonides et al., 2023; Sheehan and Serences, 2022).
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's findings in relation to existing models.

claim: Serial dependence can be observed on the neural level as a distortion of current neural representations that mirrors the attractive bias in behavior.
source: This demonstrates that serial dependence can be observed on the neural level as a distortion of current neural representations that mirrors the attractive bias in behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: This direct neural signature of serial dependence emerges after encoding but prior to the response.
source: This direct neural signature of serial dependence emerges after encoding but prior to the response, thus speaking against the proposal that serial dependence is attributable to response-related processes (Hajonides et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the timing of serial dependence based on the study's findings.

claim: A positive correlation was observed between the deviations of the neural reconstruction and response errors on a single-trial level.
source: Indeed, we observed a positive correlation between the deviations of the neural reconstruction and response errors on a single-trial level.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The correlation between neural reconstruction and response errors was found during the presentation of the retro-cue, coinciding with the time point at which the neural representation of the current target stimulus was biased toward the recent past.
source: Interestingly, this correlation was found during the presentation of the retro-cue, coinciding with the time point at which the neural representation of the current target stimulus was biased toward the recent past.
evidence: This is an observation about the timing of the correlation.

claim: A reactivation of previous target information was observed during the retro-cue presentation.
source: In addition, we observed a reactivation of previous target information during the retro-cue presentation.
evidence: This is a finding from the reactivation analysis.

claim: The distortion of the current neural representation could be the result of an integration of past information.
source: The distortion of the current neural representation could thus be the result of an integration of past information.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The retro-cue period emerges as the time point when different neural markers of serial dependence appear together.
source: Taking these findings together, the retro-cue period emerges at the time point when different neural markers of serial dependence appear together.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple findings from the study.

claim: The selective read-out of memorized information for an upcoming report might be a crucial process for serial dependence during working memory.
source: This suggests that the selective read-out of memorized information for an upcoming report might be a crucial process for serial dependence during working memory.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing findings.

claim: The neural representation of S1 already became attracted toward the target of the previous trial when S2 was presented.
source: The neural representation of S1 already became attracted toward the target of the previous trial when S2 was presented.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The reconstruction of the S1 direction had dropped to baseline and reappeared during the S2 epoch.
source: Notably, the reconstruction of the S1 direction had dropped to baseline and reappeared during the S2 epoch.
evidence: This is an observation from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Memory content that has become neurally silent can be successfully reconstructed from the impulse response elicited by a 'ping' or probe stimulus.
source: This fits well with the observation that memory content that has become neurally silent can be successfully reconstructed from the impulse response elicited by a 'ping' or probe stimulus (Wolff et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The observed S1 reconstruction elicited by S2 presentation likely reflects a 'hidden state' of working memory, in which unattended information is stored.
source: Therefore, the observed S1 reconstruction elicited by S2 presentation in our study likely reflects the same type of memory read-out, which might have driven the observed neural distortion.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to prior work on hidden states.

claim: Serial dependence in behavior increases as a function of delay duration.
source: As Bliss et al., 2017 observed, serial dependence in behavior increases as a function of delay duration, so the distortion of the neural representation of S1 during the S2 period could also reflect an increasing bias during working memory maintenance.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bliss et al., 2017.

claim: Several recent studies have shown that serial dependence operates already during perception.
source: Several recent studies have shown that serial dependence operates already during perception (Manassi et al., 2018; Murai and Whitney, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In the current study, the neural representation of the current information became biased only after encoding.
source: In the current study, the neural representation of the current information became biased only after encoding.
evidence: This is a summary of the timing findings from the current study.

claim: A reactivation of previous information was observed as an indirect marker of serial dependence before and during the onset of S1.
source: However, we did observe a reactivation of previous information as an indirect marker of serial dependence before and during the onset of S1, replicating previous results (Barbosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the reactivation analysis that replicates prior work.

claim: Cicchini et al., 2021 proposed a predictive coding framework, in which priors informed by past visual input are compared against incoming visual information during early encoding.
source: Cicchini et al., 2021 proposed a predictive coding framework, in which priors informed by past visual input are compared against incoming visual information during early encoding.
evidence: This describes a theoretical framework from a cited study.

claim: According to the predictive coding framework, the comparison of priors with incoming information results in a prediction error, which determines whether a current stimulus will be biased toward the past.
source: This comparison results in a prediction error, which determines whether a current stimulus will be biased toward the past.
evidence: This describes a mechanism from the predictive coding framework.

claim: Serial dependence might operate at different levels of object processing, including early perceptual and later, memory-related processes.
source: One possibility is that serial dependence does not operate at a single but rather at different levels of object processing, including early perceptual and later, memory-related processes (Whitney et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by a citation.

claim: Perception and working memory might not be as different as they appear: both functions build mental representations from sensory input, involving feedforward and feedback processing.
source: Moreover, perception and working memory might not be as different as they appear: both functions build mental representations from sensory input, involving feedforward and feedback processing.
evidence: This is a theoretical perspective on the relationship between perception and working memory.

claim: The study demonstrates that serial dependence in working memory directly acts on memory representations and biases them toward the past.
source: In summary, our study provides a direct neural signature of serial dependence that mirrors the attractive behavioral bias. This demonstrates that serial dependence in working memory directly acts on memory representations and biases them toward the past.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The attractive distortion of the current representation happened after object encoding, suggesting that read-out processes during object decoding are important for the emergence of serial dependence.
source: The attractive distortion of the current representation happened after object encoding, suggesting that read-out processes during object decoding are important for the emergence of serial dependence.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the timing and mechanism of serial dependence based on the study's findings.

claim: Thirteen participants were recruited from the Goethe-University Frankfurt and the Fresenius University of Applied Sciences Frankfurt.
source: Thirteen participants were recruited from the Goethe-University Frankfurt and the Fresenius University of Applied Sciences Frankfurt.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: All subjects reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were screened for red–green blindness.
source: All subjects reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were screened for red–green blindness.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: The final sample consisted of 10 subjects (3 male), aged between 22 and 30 years (mean: 25.2 years).
source: This resulted in a sample of 10 subjects (3 male), aged between 22 and 30 years (mean: 25.2 years).
evidence: This describes the final participant sample.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the Goethe-University Frankfurt am Main.
source: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the Goethe-University Frankfurt am Main.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The choice for the sample size was based on a priori power calculation.
source: The choice for the sample size was based on a priori power calculation.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the sample size.

claim: Random dot patterns (RDP) consisted of 200 dots colored in red or green on a black background.
source: Random dot patterns (RDP) were presented centrally on the screen and consisted of 200 dots colored in red (RGB: 255, 0, 0) or green (RGB: 0, 86.4105, 0) on a black background.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties used in the experiment.

claim: The dots moved with a velocity of 3.5°/s and were fully coherent in a direction randomly drawn from a pool of directions between 5° and 355° spaced 10° from one another.
source: The dots moved with a velocity of 3.5°/s and were fully coherent in a direction randomly drawn from a pool of directions between 5° and 355° spaced 10° from one another, therefore avoiding cardinal directions.
evidence: This describes the motion properties of the stimuli.

claim: Each trial began with the presentation of the first stimulus (S1) for 200 ms followed by a noise mask for 100 ms.
source: Specifically, each trial began with the presentation of the first stimulus (S1) for 200 ms followed by a noise mask for 100 ms consisting of dots moving with 0% coherence (i.e., randomly) and of the same color as the preceding RDP.
evidence: This describes the trial structure of the experiment.

claim: After a 1000-ms interval (ISI), the second stimulus (S2) and its noise mask were presented for 200 and 100 ms, respectively.
source: After a 1000-ms interval (ISI), the second stimulus (S2) and its noise mask were presented for 200 and 100 ms, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the trial structure, also shown in Figure 1.

claim: Subjects were asked to memorize the motion direction of both RDP for a delay of 1000 ms.
source: Subjects were asked to memorize the motion direction of both RDP for a delay of 1000 ms.
evidence: This describes the task instructions.

claim: The fixation square changed its color to red or green for 1500 ms, thereby cueing which motion direction became a target item and had to be reported.
source: Then the fixation square changed its color to red or green for 1500 ms, thereby cueing which motion direction became a target item and had to be reported.
evidence: This describes the retro-cue procedure.

claim: MEG was recorded with a whole-head MEG system (Omega 2005; VSM MedTech Ltd, Port Coquitlam, Canada) with 275 axial gradiometers (271 active) at a sampling rate of 1200 Hz.
source: We recorded MEG with a whole-head MEG system (Omega 2005; VSM MedTech Ltd, Port Coquitlam, Canada) with 275 axial gradiometers (271 active) at a sampling rate of 1200 Hz and without online filtering.
evidence: This describes the MEG recording equipment and parameters.

claim: Electrocardiogram (ECG), vertical and horizontal electrooculograms (EOG) as well as continuous gaze position and pupil dilation of the right eye were recorded.
source: Additionally, we recorded electrocardiogram (ECG), vertical and horizontal electrooculograms (EOG) as well as continuous gaze position and pupil dilation of the right eye by an MEG-compatible eye tracker (Eyelink CL 1000, SR Research Ltd).
evidence: This describes additional physiological recordings.

claim: MEG data were preprocessed using the python-based M/EEG analysis toolbox MNE (version 0.22.0).
source: MEG data were preprocessed using the python-based M/EEG analysis toolbox MNE (version 0.22.0; Gramfort et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the software used for MEG preprocessing.

claim: The MEG signal was first notch filtered at 50 Hz and up to 250 Hz in steps of 50 Hz to remove line noise.
source: The MEG signal was first notch filtered at 50 Hz and up to 250 Hz in steps of 50 Hz to remove line noise and then cut into trials from 1000 ms before S1 onset until 500 ms after response onset.
evidence: This describes the MEG preprocessing steps.

claim: Trials containing SQUID jump artifacts were manually identified and excluded.
source: Trials containing SQUID jump artifacts were manually identified and excluded.
evidence: This describes the artifact rejection procedure.

claim: The remaining trials were high-pass filtered (1 Hz) and decomposed via independent component analysis (ICA) with the FastICA method.
source: The remaining trials were then high-pass filtered (1 Hz) and decomposed via independent component analysis (ICA) with the FastICA method implemented in MNE.
evidence: This describes the ICA decomposition procedure.

claim: ICs representing cardiac and ocular activity were identified via correlation with ECG and EOG signals.
source: The decomposition was then applied to the notch-filtered continuous data, and ICs representing cardiac and ocular activity were identified via correlation with ECG and EOG signals.
evidence: This describes the identification of artifact components.

claim: Trials were excluded in which the response error was at least 3 SDs higher than the subject's mean response error, or in which the response time exceeded 20 s.
source: First, we excluded trials in which the response error was at least 3 SDs higher than the subject's mean response error, or in which the response time exceeded 20 s, indicating potential attentional lapses.
evidence: This describes the behavioral data exclusion criteria.

claim: The first trial of each block was excluded, as serial dependence cannot occur on those trials.
source: We also excluded the first trial of each block, as serial dependence cannot occur on those trials, and demeaned the response errors by subtracting the overall mean response error of a participant from each individual response error to remove general individual response biases independent of serial dependence.
evidence: This describes the trial exclusion rationale.

claim: Response errors were demeaned by subtracting the overall mean response error of a participant from each individual response error to remove general individual response biases independent of serial dependence.
source: We also excluded the first trial of each block, as serial dependence cannot occur on those trials, and demeaned the response errors by subtracting the overall mean response error of a participant from each individual response error to remove general individual response biases independent of serial dependence.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing procedure.

claim: The derivative of a Gaussian curve (DoG) model is usually used to describe serial dependence.
source: We fitted the first derivative of a Gaussian curve DoG; for example, (1), a model which is usually used to describe serial dependence.
evidence: This describes the standard modeling approach for serial dependence.

claim: Bayesian adaptive direct search (BADS) was used to optimize the log likelihoods of the curve fitting.
source: We optimized the log likelihoods of our curve fitting using Bayesian adaptive direct search (BADS; Acerbi and Ma, 2017).
evidence: This describes the optimization method used, with a citation.

claim: To estimate the variability of the parameters a and w, the DoG curve fit was bootstrapped 1000 times.
source: To estimate the variability of the parameters a and w, we bootstrapped the DoG curve fit 1000 times, sampling the data with replacement on each iteration, and computed the standard deviation of the resulting bootstrapped distributions of a (see Fischer et al., 2020) for a similar procedure.
evidence: This describes the bootstrapping procedure for parameter estimation.

claim: Permutation tests were used to assess the significance of serial dependence on a group level.
source: To assess the significance of serial dependence on a group level, we used permutation tests, that is, we randomly inverted the signs of each participant's mean response error, fitted a new DoG model to the pooled group data, and collected the resulting amplitude parameters a in a permutation distribution.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure.

claim: The encoding model consisted of a basis set of 18 channels spanning the room of 0–360° with centers in steps of 20°.
source: Our model consisted of a basis set of 18 channels spanning the room of 0–360° with centers in steps of 20°.
evidence: This describes the IEM model structure.

claim: The channels had the shape of sinusoids raised to the 18th power.
source: The channels had the shape of sinusoids raised to the 18th power (adapted from Ester et al., 2015; Sprague, 2016).
evidence: This describes the channel tuning function, with citations.

claim: For each subject, the model was trained on one MEG session and tested on the other one in two iterations.
source: For each subject, we trained the model on one MEG session and tested it on the other one in two iterations, so that each MEG session was once training and once test data, and training and test data were independent.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure.

claim: To increase the signal-to-noise ratio, the epoched data were averaged across time bins of 100 ms.
source: To increase the signal-to-noise ratio, the epoched data were averaged across time bins of 100 ms, centered on 50 ms, 150 ms, etc. after epoch onset.
evidence: This describes the temporal averaging procedure.

claim: Fidelity greater than zero indicates an accurate reconstruction.
source: As such, 'reconstruction fidelity' is a summary metric with fidelity greater than zero indicating an accurate reconstruction (see Methods for details).
evidence: This defines the interpretation of the fidelity metric.

claim: Cluster-based permutation tests were used to identify time points with significant direction reconstruction fidelity.
source: We identified the time points in each epoch with significant direction reconstruction fidelity by computing a one-sided cluster-based permutation test (as implemented in MNE) against zero.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure for fidelity.

claim: A bootstrapping procedure was used to assess the significance of potential shifts.
source: To assess the significance of potential shifts, we used a bootstrapping procedure similar to Ester et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure for shifts, with a citation.

claim: A shift was significant when 95% of the resampling iterations led to a shift equal to or higher than 0°.
source: A shift was significant when 95% of the resampling iterations led to a shift equal to or higher than 0°, that is, we conducted a one-sided bootstrapping test as we expected an attraction, which was indicated by a shift larger than 0°.
evidence: This describes the significance criterion for the bootstrapping test.

claim: The circular correlation between the maximum of the stimulus direction reconstructions and the response error was calculated for each time point and epoch separately across single trials.
source: Specifically, we calculated the circular correlation between the maximum of the stimulus direction reconstructions and the response error for each time point and epoch separately across single trials, that is, we tested whether the shift/deviation of the neural response from the true value, for example, in the clockwise (CW) direction, was accompanied by a corresponding shift/deviation of the behavioral response.
evidence: This describes the correlation analysis procedure.

claim: An FDR correction (Benjamini–Hochberg) was applied to analyses that resulted in one p-value per epoch.
source: In order to correct for multiple comparisons, we applied an FDR correction (Benjamini–Hochberg) to those analyses that resulted in one p-value per epoch, that is, the bootstrapping tests of the shifts against zero, and reported these corrected values alongside the original ones.
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction procedure.

claim: For cluster-based permutation tests applied to each epoch individually, p-values higher than the minimally possible were multiplied by the number of epochs (3), resulting in a Bonferroni correction.
source: Furthermore, for cluster-based permutation tests that were applied to each epoch individually, we multiplied p-values higher than the minimally possible (p < 0.002) for significant clusters by the number of epochs (3), thus resulting in a Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction procedure for cluster tests.
